recent_posts.title: How we made one data layer serve the UI, the mocks, and the E2E tests
recent_posts.summary: Red Hat's Hybrid Cloud Console team built a single typed data layer shared across three consumers: the production UI, Storybook mocks, and a CLI tool for seeding and cleaning E2E test environments. By enforcing that all API client imports flow through one data layer (via ESLint rules), any API contract change propagates automatically to all consumers at compile time. The CLI uses the same API clients as the UI, prefixes test resources for isolation, and runs unconditional cleanup to prevent orphaned data. E2E tests are structured as user journeys rather than endpoint checks, covering UI, API contracts, permissions, and business logic in a single pass. The architecture is designed to eventually support operational monitoring using the same test suite.

recent_posts.title: Guardrails: Enterprise safety shields with Llama Stack
recent_posts.summary: Building enterprise AI agents requires defense-in-depth safety architecture. This post shares lessons from implementing a two-layer shield system using Llama Stack: PromptGuard (86M params, CPU-based) as the first layer for detecting prompt injections and jailbreaks, and Llama Guard 3 8B (GPU-based) as the second layer for content safety across 14 categories. Key findings include the need to exclude certain safety categories (Privacy, Specialized Advice, Code Interpreter Abuse, Self-Harm) to prevent false positives in legitimate IT workflows like employee lookups. A notable challenge arose with LangGraph-based small prompt architectures, where PromptGuard incorrectly flagged internal state machine prompts as injection attempts rather than evaluating actual user input. The post emphasizes that safety shields require careful tuning per use case and cannot simply be enabled and left unattended.

recent_posts.title: How Kagenti ADK simplifies production AI agent management
recent_posts.summary: Kagenti ADK is an open source toolkit that handles the operational complexity of running AI agents in production. It implements the Linux Foundation's Agent2Agent (A2A) protocol, providing automatic agent card generation, JSON-RPC 2.0 message handling, and mutual TLS via Istio Ambient Mesh. Beyond A2A compliance, it ships runtime services injected via dependency injection: an LLM proxy supporting 15+ providers, PostgreSQL for session state, pgvector for RAG, MCP connectors, Keycloak-based authentication with SPIFFE workload identity, OpenTelemetry-based LLM tracing, and S3-compatible file storage. A CLI handles scaffolding, local runs, and Kubernetes/OpenShift deployments. Pre-built reference agents demonstrate integration patterns including two-stage retrieval, trajectory tracing, and citation rendering.

recent_posts.title: Deploy hosted control planes with OpenShift Virtualization: Distributed hosting
recent_posts.summary: This final part of a three-part series covers a distributed three-cluster architecture for deploying hosted control planes with OpenShift Virtualization. Cluster A hosts Red Hat Advanced Cluster Management as a lightweight governance hub, Cluster B runs the multicluster engine for Kubernetes and hosts control plane pods, and Cluster C provides dedicated OpenShift Virtualization infrastructure for NodePool VMs. The guide walks through prerequisites, node sizing, LVM storage configuration, MetalLB setup, and the exact hcp create cluster command with infra-namespace and infra-kubeconfig flags that route NodePool VMs to Cluster C. This topology enables maximum isolation, independent scaling of control planes and worker VMs, and multi-security-zone deployments, but comes with added operational overhead of managing three production clusters.

recent_posts.title: How to monitor Openshift Virtualization VMs with Zabbix
recent_posts.summary: Step-by-step guide for monitoring OpenShift Virtualization VMs using Zabbix integrated with Prometheus/Thanos. Covers creating a ServiceAccount with cluster-monitoring-view permissions, configuring Zabbix host groups and templates, and setting up Low Level Discovery (LLD) rules to automatically discover VMs and nodes. Includes item prototypes for CPU, memory, and network metrics using PromQL queries against the Thanos API, trigger prototypes for capacity alerts, and graph prototypes for visualization. An XML template is available for download as a starting base.

recent_posts.title: How StatefulSet deployments tripled OpenShift Pipelines throughput
recent_posts.summary: OpenShift Pipelines 1.20 introduces StatefulSet-based controller deployments as an alternative to the traditional leader election HA pattern. By using hash-based sharding (hash(key) % N), each controller pod gets a stable identity and processes a deterministic subset of PipelineRuns, enabling all replicas to actively participate in work. Benchmarks running 1,000 PipelineRuns at concurrency levels from 50 to 200 show 3–5.6× faster execution compared to leader election, with ~2× lower scheduling delays and 4× higher concurrent processing capacity. The trade-off is a slight memory increase (~12%). Enabling StatefulSet mode requires a single kubectl patch to the TektonConfig resource, with buckets and replicas values set to match.

recent_posts.title: Boosting speed: Use eBPF and netstacklat to troubleshoot latency
recent_posts.summary: netstacklat is an eBPF-powered monitoring tool that measures how long received packets sit in the Linux network stack before being read by an application. By attaching eBPF probes at multiple points in the kernel's network path (ip-start, tcp-start, tcp-socket-enqueued, tcp-socket-read), it pinpoints where latency is introduced. A practical demo shows an nginx server struggling at 9,000 RPS with 100ms+ response times; netstacklat reveals the bottleneck is nginx worker saturation, not the network. After scaling workers from 2 to 6, throughput hits 15,000 RPS with sub-2ms responses. A second investigation uncovers 10,000 redundant nftables rules adding ~87us of pre-TCP latency, which disappears after removal. The tool can run interactively or export metrics to Prometheus via ebpf_exporter.

recent_posts.title: How we turned Storybook into a behavioral verification engine
recent_posts.summary: Red Hat's team transformed Storybook from a component playground into a full behavioral verification engine for their Hybrid Cloud Console access management UI. Using Mock Service Worker (MSW) to intercept HTTP at the network boundary, they built a system of typed handler factories, seed constants, shared interaction helpers, and step-isolated journey stories. 959 specifications run in CI on every change, catching regressions across large refactors. Beyond code quality, the hosted Storybook environment became a shared artifact for design reviews, product walkthroughs, and stakeholder demos — replacing staging and screen recordings with live, accurate component behavior.

recent_posts.title: Build .NET container images with Tekton
recent_posts.summary: A walkthrough for building and pushing .NET container images using Tekton pipelines without a Dockerfile. The dotnet-publish-image Tekton task leverages the .NET SDK's built-in container publishing support. The guide covers installing the required tasks, setting up quay.io credentials as a Kubernetes Secret, defining a minimal two-step pipeline (git-clone + dotnet-publish-image), running it via a PipelineRun with a volumeClaimTemplate, and optionally triggering it automatically on Git push using Tekton Triggers with an EventListener, TriggerBinding, and TriggerTemplate.

recent_posts.title: Exploring distroless containers with Project Hummingbird
recent_posts.summary: Project Hummingbird is a collection of minimal, hardened, distroless container images from Red Hat aimed at near-zero CVEs. Unlike standard Docker Hub images, Hummingbird images strip out shells, package manager binaries, and unnecessary tools while retaining an RPM database for security scanning. Key characteristics include: no shell access (requiring podman export for inspection), more image layers due to chunkah rechunking for better layer sharing, builder variants for multi-stage builds, and SBOM support via cosign. Practical examples cover running MariaDB and NGINX containers, noting differences like NGINX listening on port 8080 instead of 80 due to non-root process requirements. The post also clarifies common misconceptions — layer count and binary count are not reliable security indicators — and positions Hummingbird as one part of a broader secure software supply chain strategy.
